title: The Great Depression: When the World's Economy Collapsed
subtitle: How a stock market crash in 1929 led to the worst economic crisis in modern history, affecting millions worldwide including Australians.

sections.heading: What Is the Stock Market? (The Basics)
sections.content:
Imagine your school needs money to build a new library. Instead of borrowing from a bank, the school sells pieces of ownership called shares or stocks to people in the community. If you buy one share, you own a tiny piece of the school. If the school becomes more valuable (maybe it gets famous for something), your share becomes worth more money, and you can sell it for a profit.

The stock market is just a big marketplace where people buy and sell these ownership pieces of companies. In the 1920s, the Australian and American stock markets were booming—everyone wanted to buy shares because companies were making lots of money and share prices kept going up.

People thought: 'If I buy a share today for $100, it'll be worth $150 next month, and I'll make $50 profit!' This made everyone excited to invest.

sections.heading: Buying on Margin: Borrowing Money to Gamble
sections.content:
Here's where things got risky. Most people didn't have enough cash to buy shares, so they borrowed money from banks or brokers (people who sell shares). This is called buying on margin.

Let's say a share costs $100. You only have $20, so you borrow $80 from a broker. You buy the share, hoping it'll go to $150. If it does, you sell it, pay back the $80, and keep $70 profit. Sounds great!

But what if the share price drops to $50? Now you owe $80 but your share is only worth $50. You've lost money you don't even have. Millions of people did this in the 1920s, betting that share prices would keep rising forever. They were wrong.

sections.heading: October 1929: The Stock Market Crash
sections.content:
In October 1929, something spooked investors. Maybe they realised share prices were too high. Maybe there were rumours of trouble ahead. Whatever the reason, people started selling their shares in panic.

When everyone sells at once, prices collapse like a house of cards. On 'Black Tuesday' (29 October 1929), the American stock market lost about 12% of its value in a single day. Imagine if your pocket money dropped by 12% overnight—that's how shocking this was.

People who'd borrowed money to buy shares were now in huge trouble. They owed money they couldn't pay back. Banks that had lent them money were also in trouble. The crash spread from America to stock markets around the world, including Australia.

sections.heading: Bank Runs: When Everyone Wants Their Money at Once
sections.content:
Here's how banks normally work: you deposit your money, and the bank lends most of it out to other people (for mortgages, business loans, etc.). The bank keeps only a small amount in cash, expecting that not everyone will want their money on the same day.

After the stock market crash, people panicked. They thought banks might collapse, so they rushed to withdraw all their money at once. This is called a bank run. But banks didn't have enough cash—they'd lent it all out! Banks started failing, and people lost their life savings.

This was catastrophic. Imagine if your parents' savings just disappeared because their bank ran out of money. Millions of families experienced this.

sections.heading: Why Did Unemployment Reach 25%?
sections.content:
When the stock market crashed, people stopped buying things. Companies couldn't sell their products, so they laid off workers. Unemployed people had no money to buy things, so more companies failed and laid off more workers. This is called a downward spiral—each problem makes the next problem worse.

In America, unemployment reached 25% by 1933. That means 1 in 4 people couldn't find a job. In Australia, it hit 30%—even worse. Imagine if three of your four best friends' parents had no job and no income.

Without jobs, families couldn't pay rent or buy food. Homelessness increased. Suicide rates went up. This wasn't just an economic problem—it was a human tragedy.

sections.heading: Deflation: When Money Becomes More Valuable (But That's Bad)
sections.content:
You might think: 'If prices drop, that's good—things are cheaper!' But during the Great Depression, deflation (when prices fall across the whole economy) was actually terrible.

Here's why: imagine you borrowed $1,000 to buy a car when prices were normal. Now prices drop 30%, and your salary drops too. You still owe $1,000, but it's now worth much more in today's money. You're paying back more than you borrowed, in real terms. People with debts got crushed.

Also, if you think prices will keep dropping, you don't buy anything today—you wait for cheaper prices tomorrow. This means companies sell even less, lay off more workers, and the economy gets worse. Deflation is like quicksand: the more you struggle, the deeper you sink.

sections.heading: The Dust Bowl: Nature's Disaster Made Worse by Economics
sections.content:
While the economy was collapsing, American farmers faced another disaster. In the 1930s, severe drought hit the Great Plains (the farming heartland of America). Without rain, crops died.

Farmers had borrowed heavily during the 1920s boom, expecting good harvests. When crops failed, they couldn't pay back loans. Banks foreclosed (took back) their farms. Desperate farmers ploughed up native grassland to plant more crops, hoping to recover losses. This made soil erosion worse.

Wind storms picked up the loose soil and created massive dust clouds—some so thick you couldn't see across the street. Thousands of families abandoned their farms and migrated west to California, looking for work. This human suffering was captured in songs and stories that Australians learned about in school.

sections.heading: Australia's Wool and Wheat Crisis
sections.content:
Australia was hit especially hard because our economy depended on exporting wool and wheat. When the Depression hit, demand for these products collapsed. Wool prices fell by 50%. Wheat prices crashed even harder.

Farmers who'd invested in land and equipment couldn't sell their products for enough money to cover costs. Unemployment in Australia reached 30%—worse than America. In some towns, nearly everyone was out of work.

Australian cities like Sydney and Melbourne had breadlines (queues of hungry people waiting for free food). Families lived in makeshift camps called 'Hoovervilles' (named mockingly after President Hoover). The Depression hit Australia's working-class communities especially hard.

sections.heading: President Hoover's Response: 'Wait It Out'
sections.content:
When the Depression started, American President Herbert Hoover believed the economy would fix itself. He thought the government shouldn't interfere too much—businesses and people should just work through the problem.

Hoover believed in rugged individualism: the idea that people should solve their own problems without government help. He thought giving people welfare (government money) would make them lazy. So he did very little to help unemployed people or struggling businesses.

This approach failed badly. The economy got worse, not better. By 1932, Hoover was deeply unpopular. Americans felt abandoned by their government while they starved.

sections.heading: Franklin D. Roosevelt and the New Deal: Fighting Back
sections.content:
In 1932, Americans elected Franklin D. Roosevelt (FDR) as president. FDR believed the government had to act decisively. His plan was called the New Deal—a massive government program to create jobs, help the poor, and restart the economy.

The New Deal created hundreds of government programs. The WPA (Works Progress Administration) hired millions of unemployed people to build roads, bridges, schools, and parks. The CCC (Civilian Conservation Corps) hired young men to plant forests and prevent soil erosion. The SSA (Social Security Administration) created pensions for elderly people and disabled people.

These programs weren't perfect, but they gave people hope and income. They also built infrastructure (roads, dams, electricity networks) that helped America modernise. FDR's approach was called fiscal policy—using government spending to influence the economy.

sections.heading: Protectionism and Tariffs: Countries Fighting Each Other
sections.content:
As the Depression worsened, countries tried to protect their own industries. They introduced tariffs—taxes on imported goods—to make foreign products more expensive and encourage people to buy local products.

America passed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff in 1930, which put huge taxes on imported goods. Other countries retaliated with their own tariffs. International trade collapsed. This made the Depression worse, not better, because countries couldn't sell their exports.

Australia also raised tariffs to protect local industries. But this backfired because Australia depended on exporting wool and wheat. When other countries raised tariffs, they bought less Australian wool and wheat. Protectionism is like a trade war—everyone loses.

sections.heading: How World War II Ended the Depression
sections.content:
The Depression lasted about 10 years (1929-1939). It didn't end because of government programs or economic recovery—it ended because of World War II.

When WWII started in 1939, governments needed weapons, uniforms, vehicles, and food. Factories that had been closed started running again. Unemployed people got jobs making weapons and supplies. America wasn't even in the war until 1941, but American factories were already booming producing supplies for Britain and the Soviet Union.

By 1941, American unemployment had dropped from 25% to about 10%. By 1943, it was nearly zero. The war created massive demand for industrial production. It's tragic that it took a world war to end the Depression, but that's what happened.

sections.heading: Australia's Recovery and War Economy
sections.content:
Australia's economy also recovered through WWII. When Japan entered the war in 1941, Australia was directly threatened. The government mobilised the entire economy for war production.

Factories that made consumer goods switched to making weapons and ammunition. Farms that struggled during the Depression now had guaranteed markets for wheat and wool—the military needed to feed and clothe soldiers. Unemployment disappeared as people joined the military or worked in war industries.

Australian cities were transformed. Rationing (limiting how much people could buy) was introduced. Women entered the workforce in large numbers for the first time. The Depression was finally over, but only because the world was at war.

sections.heading: Long-Term Changes: What the Depression Taught Us
sections.content:
The Great Depression changed how governments think about economics. Before 1929, most governments believed in laissez-faire economics—the idea that markets should be left alone to work themselves out.

After the Depression, governments realised they needed to regulate financial markets and help people during economic crises. Australia and other countries created unemployment benefits, pensions, and welfare systems. Central banks (like the Reserve Bank of Australia) learned to manage money supply more carefully to prevent deflation.

The Depression also showed that protectionism doesn't work. After WWII, countries created international trade organisations to prevent trade wars. These lessons shaped the modern economy we live in today.

key_concepts.definition: A piece of ownership in a company. If you own one share of a company with 1,000 shares, you own 1/1000th of that company.
key_concepts.context: People bought shares hoping prices would rise, but when the market crashed in 1929, share prices collapsed and people lost fortunes.

key_concepts.definition: A sudden, dramatic fall in share prices across the whole market, usually caused by panic selling.
key_concepts.context: The October 1929 crash wiped out fortunes overnight and triggered the Great Depression.

key_concepts.definition: Borrowing money from a broker to buy shares, betting that prices will rise so you can repay the loan and keep the profit.
key_concepts.context: Millions of people did this in the 1920s. When prices fell, they owed money they couldn't repay, causing financial ruin.

key_concepts.definition: A general fall in prices across the whole economy. The opposite of inflation (rising prices).
key_concepts.context: During the Depression, deflation made debts harder to repay and discouraged people from spending, making the economy worse.

key_concepts.definition: The percentage of people who want to work but cannot find a job.
key_concepts.context: Unemployment reached 25% in America and 30% in Australia during the Depression, causing widespread poverty.

key_concepts.definition: Government decisions about spending and taxation to influence the economy.
key_concepts.context: FDR's New Deal was fiscal policy—the government spent money on public works to create jobs and stimulate the economy.

key_concepts.definition: Central bank decisions about money supply and interest rates to influence the economy.
key_concepts.context: Central banks made mistakes during the Depression by tightening money supply, making deflation worse.

key_concepts.definition: A tax on imported goods, making foreign products more expensive than local products.
key_concepts.context: Countries raised tariffs during the Depression to protect local industries, but this backfired by reducing international trade.

key_concepts.definition: Government policies designed to protect local industries from foreign competition.
key_concepts.context: Protectionist tariffs made the Depression worse by reducing trade between countries.

key_concepts.definition: When many people rush to withdraw their money from a bank at the same time, usually because they fear the bank will fail.
key_concepts.context: Bank runs during the Depression caused banks to collapse because they didn't have enough cash to pay everyone.

key_concepts.definition: When a bank takes back property (like a house or farm) from someone who can't repay their loan.
key_concepts.context: During the Depression, banks foreclosed on farms and homes, leaving families homeless.

key_concepts.definition: FDR's massive government program (1933-1939) that created jobs, provided welfare, and regulated financial markets.
key_concepts.context: The New Deal didn't end the Depression, but it reduced suffering and changed how governments respond to economic crises.

timeline.event: The 'Roaring Twenties'—economies booming, stock prices rising, people buying shares on margin, everyone optimistic about the future.
Stock prices reach their peak. Smart investors start selling, sensing trouble ahead.
'Black Thursday'—stock market drops 11% in a single day as panic selling begins.
'Black Tuesday'—the worst day, with 12% drop. The crash spreads to stock markets worldwide, including Australia.
Bank runs occur as people rush to withdraw savings. Thousands of banks fail. Unemployment rises dramatically.
America passes Smoot-Hawley Tariff. Other countries retaliate with their own tariffs. International trade collapses.
The Dust Bowl—severe drought in American Great Plains causes massive crop failures and soil erosion. Farmers lose farms.
American unemployment reaches 25%. Franklin D. Roosevelt elected president, promising the New Deal.
FDR takes office and launches New Deal programs. Government creates jobs through WPA, CCC, and other agencies.
New Deal programs reduce suffering but don't fully end the Depression. Unemployment remains high.
World War II begins in Europe. Demand for weapons and supplies increases. Factories start rehiring workers.
America enters WWII. Full industrial mobilisation begins. Unemployment drops sharply as war production ramps up.
American unemployment nearly reaches zero. The Great Depression is effectively over, replaced by wartime economy.

why_it_still_matters: The Great Depression taught governments that they must regulate financial markets and help people during economic crises. Today's unemployment benefits, pensions, and financial regulations exist because of lessons learned in the 1930s. When the 2008 financial crisis hit, governments used fiscal and monetary policies to prevent another depression. Understanding the Depression helps us understand why governments respond to economic problems the way they do today, and why we have safety nets like welfare and unemployment payments.
discussion_questions: If you could go back to 1929 and warn one person about the stock market crash, who would it be and what would you tell them? What might have changed?
Some people say the government shouldn't help unemployed people because it makes them lazy. Others say the government must help or people will starve. What do you think, and why?

Australia's economy depended on exporting wool and wheat. Today, Australia still depends heavily on exporting resources like iron ore and coal. What could happen if demand for these exports suddenly collapsed? How is Australia different now?
The Depression ended because of WWII, not because of economic recovery. Is it fair to say the war 'solved' the Depression? What does this tell us about the limits of economic policy?
During the Depression, countries raised tariffs to protect their industries, but this made things worse. Why do you think countries still use tariffs today, even though we know they can backfire?
If a similar stock market crash happened today, how might it be different from 1929? (Think about: social media, government regulations, international trade, technology)
